story: Alaska DNR issues its Final Finding and Decision approving a 50-year lease for STAK Energy's gas-powered North Slope data center campus, with a tiered Compute Power Sales Surcharge

source_fetch_summary.notes: Counts are WebFetch requests only. 5 succeeded (alaskapublic.org, eia.gov, two adn.com articles, waymo.com). 1 failed (law.cornell.edu 11 AAC 02.040 returned only an index page and is not cited). The DNR PDF was not fetched with WebFetch. The showrunner pulled it today with scripts/fetch_pdf_text.py, and its text layer at /home/user/alaskaaicarousels/out/2026-11-11/pdfs/stak_ffd.txt was read as that URL's response. Curly apostrophes in PDF quotes have been changed to straight ones, and line-break hyphen or space artifacts are noted where they occur.

claims.claim: Alaska DNR issued its Final Finding and Decision on ADL 422741 for STAK Energy Corporation on November 10th.
claims.verbatim: STAK ENERGY CORPORATION ADL 422741 Final Finding and Decision AS 38.05.070(d) November 10, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: stak_ffd.txt lines 11-14. The PDF has 102 pages including attachments. FFD pages 22-23 (the signature page) are a scan with no text layer. November 10th fell on a Tuesday, which matches the Alaska Beacon's 'on Tuesday approved' (C48).

claims.claim: The decision finds that issuing STAK a 50-year negotiated lease is in the State's best interest.
claims.verbatim: This FFD constitutes the Department's final determination that it is in the State's best interest to issue a 50-year negotiated lease to STAK.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 59-60, with the same finding at lines 20-23 under AS 38.05.070(d). Lines 24-28 say STAK may apply to renew and renewal is not guaranteed. The Attachment E Division Response (lines 3547-3549) says the statute allows up to 55 years. The decision is not yet final against challenge, since a 20-day reconsideration period applies (C49).

claims.claim: The project site lies about one mile west of the Dalton Highway at Milepost 390.
claims.verbatim: The project site is located approximately one mile west of the Dalton Highway at Milepost 390, west of both the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation (AGDC) right -of-way
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 78-79, also lines 40-41. The site is west of TAPS and inside the North Slope Borough (line 87).

claims.claim: The lease covers approximately 715.4 acres of state surface estate.
claims.verbatim: on approximately 715.4 acres of State of Alaska surface estate located approximately 26 miles south of Deadhorse, Alaska.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 527-528. Also line 128 and the lease agreement at line 2717 ('containing approximately 715.4 acres'). Lines 533-539 say this is the gross lease area and not the disturbed acreage. The planned principal gravel pad is about 640 to 650 acres. The Alaska Beacon rounds this to 'about 715 acres'.

claims.claim: The lease site is approximately 26 miles south of Deadhorse.
claims.verbatim: on approximately 715.4 acres of State of Alaska surface estate located approximately 26 miles south of Deadhorse, Alaska.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 527-528. Attachment E (line 4277) says 'approximately 26 road miles from Deadhorse', so treat this as a road distance.

claims.claim: The planned natural gas-fired power system is designed to produce 1 to 3 gigawatts of electricity.
claims.verbatim: a natural gas -fired power generation system designed to produce 1- 3 giga watts (GW) of electrical power
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 547-548. The text layer splits 'gigawatts' and spaces the hyphen. Line 632 repeats '1-3 GW gas-fired facility'. This is a design figure, not built capacity.

claims.claim: The lease grant authorizes generation facilities with aggregate capacity up to three gigawatts to support hyperscale data centers and artificial intelligence computing facilities.
claims.verbatim: an integrated energy campus consisting of one or more electric generation facilities with an aggregate capacity up to three gigawatts and all associated infrastructure necessary to support hyperscale data centers, artificial intelligence computing facilities
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lease agreement grant clause at lines 2708-2711, quoted in the FFD at lines 836-840. The attached lease is a form with dates and signatures still blank (line 2673).

claims.claim: DNR received 1,205 public comments on the preliminary decision between May 12th and July 17th.
claims.verbatim: DNR received 1,205 comments between May 12, 2026 and July 17, 2026, a volume that demonstrates significant public engagement with the available material.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 396-397, also line 371 and Attachment E line 3337. Footnote 13 (lines 403-404) splits it into 528 comments in the first period and 677 in the extension. The Alaska Beacon's 'more than 1,200 public responses' agrees.

claims.claim: STAK's March 12th revised application raised the projected construction workforce from up to 500 to up to 1,500 workers.
claims.verbatim: an increase in the projected construction workforce from up to 500 to up to 1,500 workers
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 283-285. The same revision renamed the project from 'STAK Energy Datacenter Project' to 'STAK Energy Campus'.

claims.claim: The revised application replaced the earlier modular data center units with planned high-performance computing units.
claims.verbatim: updated facility descriptions reflecting the planned use of HPC units in lieu of the previously described modular data center units
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 286-288. Line 246 defines HPC as high-performance computing. The revision also added a possible natural gas treatment and compression system (lines 288).

claims.claim: Construction is expected to need a peak workforce of up to 1,500 workers.
claims.verbatim: Construction is expected to require a peak workforce of up to 1,500 workers
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: expected to need up to 1,500 construction workers at peak
claims.notes: Lines 585-586. This is STAK's projection, cited to its CIA.

claims.claim: Ongoing operations are anticipated to employ between 50 and 150 permanent personnel.
claims.verbatim: ongoing operations are anticipated to employ between 50 and 150 permanent personnel on rotating shifts.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: anticipated to employ 50 to 150 permanent staff, according to STAK's cumulative impact analysis
claims.notes: Lines 586-587, repeated at line 736. Footnote 37 (lines 610-612) is a disputed figure. STAK's Development Plan says a permanent workforce of up to 60, and DNR used the CIA's 50 to 150 range. Mention the disagreement or hedge the number.

claims.claim: Construction capital expenditures are estimated at approximately $500 million.
claims.verbatim: Construction capital expenditures of approximately $500 million will generate significant economic activity throughout Alaska
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: about $500 million in construction spending, according to STAK's application
claims.notes: Line 733, citing STAK's Application at 4 (footnote 49). Attachment E line 4201 says 'STAK, not the State, bears the roughly $500 million in construction costs'. This is the applicant's estimate and should be attributed to STAK.

claims.claim: The project will not be interconnected to the Railbelt or any other existing Alaska utility network.
claims.verbatim: This project is not interconnected to the Railbelt or any other existing Alaska utility network.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Line 577. Lines 575-576 describe it as behind-the-meter. Attachment E lines 4382-4383 agree. The Alaska Beacon says it 'would not be tied into the electrical grid that covers Alaska's Railbelt'. ADN's republication adds that operators could sell power to customers in and around Prudhoe Bay.

claims.claim: The project is to be built in phases over an estimated six-year buildout period.
claims.verbatim: The project will be developed in phases over an estimated six-year buildout period
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: expected to take about six years to build
claims.notes: Line 579. Lines 580-583 call the schedule preliminary. The Alaska Beacon writes 'Construction on the privately financed project is expected to take six years.'

claims.claim: Fuel use at full operating capacity is anticipated at 350 to 500 million standard cubic feet of gas per day.
claims.verbatim: Estimated fuel consumption at full operational capacity is anticipated at a range of 350-500 million standard cubic feet per day (MMscf/day)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: estimated to burn 350 to 500 million cubic feet of gas a day at full capacity
claims.notes: Lines 569-571, subject to final turbine selection. This is an estimate from STAK's CIA. The gas pipeline is outside this lease and needs its own right-of-way application (lines 572-574).

claims.claim: DNR says the lease would support the first gigawatt scale data center project in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: The proposed lease would support the first gigawatt scale data center project in Alaska.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: what DNR calls Alaska's first gigawatt-scale data center project
claims.notes: Lines 941-942. This is DNR's own description, so attribute it to DNR.

claims.claim: The final lease combines a Base Rate set by appraised land value with an additional Compute Power Sales Surcharge.
claims.verbatim: The final lease incorporates both a Base Rate established by the appraised market value of the land and an additional Compute Power Sales Surcharge (Surcharge) based on the amount of electricity produced on the leased parcel
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 966-968. Lease section 1 (lines 2728-2730) and EA item 45 (lines 2530-2532) agree. The legal basis is AS 38.05.073(m) and 38.05.075(f) (lines 935-964).

claims.claim: The May preliminary decision had contemplated that additional rental might be based on a percentage of gross receipts.
claims.verbatim: The PD contemplated that an additional rental might be based on a percentage of gross receipts.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 970-971. Lines 969-970 say the FFD's compensation framework is more specific than the PD's, 'Following review and negotiations with the Applicant'. The PD is dated May 12th (line 17).

claims.claim: DNR says the Surcharge is designed to work like a gross-receipts approach while being simpler to administer and verify.
claims.verbatim: The Surcharge is designed to provide a compensation structure similar to a gross -receipts-based approach while allowing for simpler administration, monitoring, and verification.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 971 and 979-981, across a page break. Lines 983-986 say metered electricity delivered to the data center serves 'as a proxy for project revenue'.

claims.claim: Compute power sales means the megawatt-hours of electricity generated on the leased premises, metered, and delivered to any data center, compute facility or other computing infrastructure.
claims.verbatim: Compute power sales means the megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity generated on the leased premises, metered, and delivered to any data center, compute facility, or other computing infrastructure.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Definition from the Entry Authorization (Attachment C), item 45.e.i, lines 2559-2561. It appears word for word in the proposed lease, section 1.d.i, lines 2754-2757.

claims.claim: Surcharge Tier 1 covers 0 to 876,000 MWh of annual compute power sales, equivalent to an average load under 100 MW, at $0.00 per MWh.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Table row at EA line 2563 and lease line 2760, with whitespace collapsed. Column headers (line 2562) are 'Tier', 'Annual Compute Power Sales (MWh per Lease Year)', 'Equivalent Average Compute Load (MW)' and 'Surcharge Rate ($ per MWh)'. Unit check: 876,000 MWh over 8,760 hours is 100 MW, so the columns agree.

claims.claim: Surcharge Tier 2 covers 876,001 to 4,380,000 MWh a year, equivalent to 100 to 500 MW, at $0.20 per MWh.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA line 2564 and lease line 2761. Unit check: 4,380,000 MWh over 8,760 hours is 500 MW.

claims.claim: Surcharge Tier 3 covers 4,380,001 to 8,760,000 MWh a year, equivalent to 500 to 1,000 MW, at $0.40 per MWh.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA line 2565 and lease line 2762. This is the highest rate in the schedule. Unit check: 8,760,000 MWh over 8,760 hours is 1,000 MW.

claims.claim: Surcharge Tier 4 covers 8,760,001 to 13,140,000 MWh a year, equivalent to 1,000 to 1,500 MW, at $0.30 per MWh.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA line 2566 and lease line 2763. Unit check: 13,140,000 MWh over 8,760 hours is 1,500 MW.

claims.claim: Surcharge Tier 5 covers 13,140,001 to 20,699,880 MWh a year, equivalent to 1,500 to 2,363 MW, at $0.16 per MWh.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA line 2567 and lease line 2764. Unit check: 20,699,880 MWh over 8,760 hours is exactly 2,363 MW. The top tier ends below the 3 GW nameplate because the tiers track expected deliveries to compute and not generating capacity (C32).

claims.claim: Each surcharge rate applies only to the compute power sales within its own tier, and moving into a new tier does not change the charge on lower tiers.
claims.verbatim: each surcharge rate applies only to the Compute Power Sales within its respective tier, and moving into a new tier does not affect the surcharge calculation for Compute Power Sales in lower tiers.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 993-994. Lease section 1.d (lines 2744-2746) says the Surcharge is calculated annually on the lease year's cumulative actual compute power sales and is due 90 days after the lease year ends.

claims.claim: DNR says surcharge rates decline at larger scales to encourage continued investment toward full buildout.
claims.verbatim: At larger scales, the surcharge rates decline to encourage continued investment and development toward the project's full planned buildout.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1008-1010. The text layer reads 'contin ued' with a stray space, here closed up. This is DNR's stated reason, so attribute it to DNR. It matches the table, where rates rise to $0.40 in Tier 3 and then fall to $0.30 and $0.16.

claims.claim: No surcharge is assessed in the first tier, where only the Base Rate applies.
claims.verbatim: The Base Rate applies at the initial tier to ensure that minimum rent requirements are met, however, no surcharge is assessed during this tier, providing the project an opportunity to establish operations
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas

claims.claim: The Base Rate is the minimum annual payment and is credited against any Surcharge due in the same period, with STAK paying only the difference.
claims.verbatim: The Base Rate shall constitute a minimum annual payment and be credited against the amount of any Surcharge due during a payment period. To the extent the Surcharge exceeds the Base Rate, STAK will pay the difference.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1020-1023. Lease section 1.h (lines 2784-2791) and EA item 45.i (lines 2592-2598) agree. The Base Rate is set by a formal appraisal at STAK's expense (lines 1016-1017), and it is not yet known.

claims.claim: If the Surcharge for a period is less than the Base Rate, STAK gets no refund, credit or carryforward.
claims.verbatim: If the Surcharge for a payment period is less than the Base Rate, no refund, credit, or carryforward shall be provided to the Lessee.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA lines 2599-2600 and lease lines 2795-2797.

claims.claim: The surcharge tiers were built on anticipated compute power sales at full buildout rather than on the project's nameplate generating capacity.
claims.verbatim: the surcharge tiers were developed based on anticipated Compute Power Sales at full buildout rather than the project's nameplate generating capacity.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 996-998. Lines 998-1001 say part of generation is held back for redundancy, reliability and maintenance.

claims.claim: STAK may ask to reopen the Surcharge if the State changes a law or policy that directly affects the project's economics.
claims.verbatim: the State adopts a change in law or policy that directly affects the project's economics, the Lessee may request that the Compute Power Sales Surcharge be reopened for limited, good faith renegotiation.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: EA lines 2602-2607 and lease lines 2799-2806. A change must not cut total compensation below fair market value. The FFD body describes this at lines 1010-1012.

claims.claim: An advance rental of $10 per acre per year applies during the Entry Authorization.
claims.verbatim: During the term of the EA, an advanced rental of $10 per acre per year will be in effect.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1040-1042, also EA item 45.a at lines 2541-2542. The showrunner should state any per-year dollar total for the parcel as its own declared aggregate.

claims.claim: The five-year Entry Authorization counts inside the 50-year lease term and does not extend it.
claims.verbatim: the lease term of 50 years begins when the EA is signed, and the five years of EA will not extend the overall length of the authorization beyond 50 years
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1042-1046. Line 1042 says 'The term of the EA will be five years and will be issued after this FFD goes into effect.'

claims.claim: Any sublease must first be approved in writing by DNR.
claims.verbatim: All potential subleases must first be approved in writing by the Department, and the Department may conduct further agency review and/or public notice
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1063-1066. Lease section 1.j (lines 2810-2812) adds that 'Additional compensation to the State may be required as a condition of approval.'

claims.claim: DNR says agreements with energy offtakers do not, merely by existing, count as a sublease of state land.
claims.verbatim: agreements with energy offtakers may be integral to the financing and commercial viability of an energy-intensive project. Such agreements do not, merely by virtue of their existence, constitute a sublease
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 1070-1072. The text layer reads 'integral t o', here closed up. Lines 1073-1075 say DNR will judge the substance of each arrangement under AS 38.05.095.

claims.claim: STAK must post an initial performance guaranty totaling $1,250,000.
claims.verbatim: in the amount of $250,000 prior to entry onto the site under the terms of the EA. Prior to gravel placement in support of construction of the gravel pad or road, an additional $1,000,000 will be required, for an initial performance guaranty totaling $1,250,000.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 895-898. The total is stated in the document and was not computed here. A separate Financial Assurance Agreement is required before the final lease (lines 900-906).

claims.claim: STAK's cumulative impact analysis estimates dry air cooling will cut direct operational water use by 90 percent or more compared with evaporative cooling.
claims.verbatim: STAK's Cumulative Impact Analysis (CIA) estimates that this approach will reduce direct operational water consumption by 90 percent or more compared to evaporative cooling at lower-latitude data centers.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: the developer estimates air cooling will cut direct water use by 90 percent or more
claims.notes: Attachment E (Responses to Public Comments), Division Response to Topic 2.1, lines 3715-3719. This is the developer's estimate, so it has to be attributed. Operational water demand is put at 'tens of thousands of gallons per day' (lines 3719-3722). The Alaska Beacon quotes the same 90 percent phrase.

claims.claim: DNR says the facility will be visible from the Dalton Highway at roughly one mile.
claims.verbatim: The facility will be visible from the Dalton Highway at roughly one mile and will operate a 1-3 gigawatt generation system
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Attachment E, Topic 3.2 Division Response, lines 3959-3960. The Alaska Beacon has the identical sentence.

claims.claim: DNR's Division of Oil and Gas says it is not the agency responsible for setting or enforcing greenhouse gas emission standards.
claims.verbatim: The Division is not the agency responsible for establishing or enforcing greenhouse gas emission standards, conducting statewide climate monitoring, or making technical determinations regarding the causes, extent, or future trajectory of climate change.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Attachment E, Topic 7.1, lines 4469-4471. In the same response (lines 4462-4463) the Division acknowledges the facility 'would generate greenhouse gas emissions'. So do not write that DNR ignored emissions. It deferred standards to other agencies. The Alaska Beacon quotes the first clause.

claims.claim: DNR says it is not obligated to conduct a general corporate or financial investigation of STAK beyond what bears on its best interest decision.
claims.verbatim: The Division is not, however, obligated to conduct a general corporate or financial investigation beyond what bears on the decision of whether the proposed disposal is in the best interest of the State.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Attachment E, Topic 1.2, lines 3528-3530. Lines 3473-3476 say STAK treats its financing and investor details as confidential. Lines 3522-3523 say DNR 'has not received that kind of comprehensive financial and corporate disclosure'. The Alaska Beacon quotes this phrase.

claims.claim: STAK says the lease area is approximately 60 air miles from Nuiqsut, the nearest permanent community.
claims.verbatim: The proposed lease area is located approximately 60 air miles from Nuiqsut, which is the nearest permanent community.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.suggested_phrasing: about 60 air miles from Nuiqsut, the nearest permanent community, according to STAK
claims.notes: This is the Applicant Response in Attachment E (lines 3630-3631, repeated at 3982-3983), so it is STAK's statement inside a DNR document. The Alaska Beacon says 'The data center will be 60 miles from the nearest inhabited town.' Deadhorse is an industrial camp about 26 road miles away (C05). Say 'permanent community' so the two distances do not contradict each other.

claims.claim: DNR's Responses to Public Comments, attached to the decision, run 30 pages.
claims.verbatim: Page 1 of 30 STAK Energy Corporation ADL 422741 Responses to Public Comments Attachment to Final Finding and Decision, AS 38.05.070
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Lines 3327-3331. The responses are grouped into eight issues (line 3349). The Alaska Beacon describes 'a 30-page response filed alongside Tuesday's approval'.

claims.claim: STAK will need a Clean Water Act Section 404 permit from the Army Corps of Engineers for wetlands, which DNR says must be resolved before construction.
claims.verbatim: STAK will be required to obtain authorization from USACE under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, which will provide additional site-specific review of jurisdictional wetlands
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Attachment E, Topic 3.2, lines 3934-3935. Lines 3930-3933 say wetland impacts are not yet set by a final delineation and must be resolved in Section 404 permitting 'prior to construction'. The Alaska Beacon lists 'a federal wetlands permit' among the approvals still required (C52).

claims.claim: DNR says the project is entirely privately financed and does not commit State appropriations.
claims.verbatim: The project as proposed is entirely privately financed and privately built.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Attachment E, Topic 4.3 Division Response, lines 4200-4203. In the same topic (lines 4189-4190) STAK says it is not seeking State appropriations or State-backed financing. The Alaska Beacon calls it 'the privately financed project'.

claims.claim: STAK expects to need a Prevention of Significant Deterioration construction permit and a Title V operating permit from DEC for air emissions.
claims.verbatim: STAK anticipates these will include a Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) construction permit and a Title V operating permit from the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Applicant Response in Attachment E, Topic 2.2, lines 3747-3750. The Alaska Beacon refers to 'a state air quality permit for the power plant'.

claims.claim: The Alaska Beacon reported that DNR approved the 50-year land lease on Tuesday.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a 50-year land lease
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Page says 'Published November 11, 2026 at 3:29 PM AKST'. The primary decision is dated November 10th, which was a Tuesday (C01). The tool returned quotes as excerpts capped at 125 characters.

claims.claim: The decision is subject to a 20-day reconsideration period.
claims.verbatim: Tuesday's decision is subject to a 20-day reconsideration period and could be challenged in court.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: subject to a 20-day reconsideration period, according to the Alaska Beacon
claims.notes: Comes from the Beacon only. The notice of reconsideration rights is probably on FFD pages 22-23, which are a scan with no text layer, so the primary could not be read. A fetch of 11 AAC 02.040 on law.cornell.edu failed (index page only). The ADN copy is the same Beacon story, so it is not independent. Attribute to the Beacon. The lease reopener at line 2608 names 11 AAC 02 as DNR's appeal framework, which fits but does not prove the 20 days.

claims.claim: The Alaska Beacon reported that the decision could be challenged in court.
claims.verbatim: Tuesday's decision is subject to a 20-day reconsideration period and could be challenged in court.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: could still be challenged in court, the Alaska Beacon reported
claims.notes: This states a possibility, not a filed case. No lawsuit is known as of the run date. Same single-source limit as C49.

claims.claim: The Alaska Beacon reported that most of the more than 1,200 public responses opposed the proposal.
claims.verbatim: received more than 1,200 public responses, most in opposition to the proposal.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.suggested_phrasing: most of them opposed, according to the Alaska Beacon
claims.notes: Fragment as returned by the tool. The count matches DNR's 1,205 (C08). The 'most in opposition' description is the Beacon's alone. DNR's documents do not tally support against opposition, and the ADN copy is not independent. Only use it attributed to the Beacon, never as the deck's own statement.

claims.claim: The Alaska Beacon reported that the project still needs further approvals, including a federal wetlands permit and a state air quality permit for the power plant.
claims.verbatim: including a federal wetlands permit and a state air quality permit for the power plant.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Fragment as returned. The primary document confirms both (C45 Section 404, C47 PSD and Title V). The FFD (lines 476-481) also says the lease does not replace any other state or federal authorization.

claims.claim: John Boyle serves as chief strategy officer for STAK Energy.
claims.verbatim: serves as chief strategy officer for STAK Energy.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Anchorage Daily News
claims.suggested_phrasing: John Boyle, STAK's chief strategy officer according to the Alaska Beacon
claims.notes: The tool returned the sentence in pieces. Full reading: 'John Boyle, who previously served as commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources under Gov. Mike Dunleavy ... and ran for state House in the Nov. 3 election ... serves as chief strategy officer for STAK Energy.' The alaskapublic.org copy fetched today does not include this sentence. Single secondary source, so attribute it. ADN page shows 'Published 5 hours ago', and the date comes from the URL path.

claims.claim: Boyle previously served as commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources under Governor Mike Dunleavy.
claims.verbatim: John Boyle, who previously served as commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources under Gov. Mike Dunleavy
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), republished by Anchorage Daily News
claims.suggested_phrasing: a former DNR commissioner, the Alaska Beacon reported
claims.notes: A named-person claim about a possible conflict of interest. Do not suggest Boyle took part in this decision, since nothing fetched says he did. The FFD text layer does not name him. Single secondary source.

claims.claim: Alaska's net electricity generation in 2024 was 6,690,506 megawatthours.
claims.verbatim: Net generation (megawatthours) 6,690,506 48
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Energy Information Administration
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, outside the news window by design. Table 1, 2024 Summary statistics, 'Data for: 2024', 'Release Date: November 10, 2025'. Today's page matches the figure from runs/2026-10-05. Alaska ranks 48th. Utilities produced 6,020,426 MWh and IPP and CHP 670,080. Same unit as the surcharge tiers (MWh per year). The showrunner should declare any ratio to the Tier 5 cap of 20,699,880 MWh as its own aggregate.

claims.claim: Alaska's net summer generating capacity in 2024 was 2,853 megawatts.
claims.verbatim: Net summer capacity (megawatts) 2,853 48
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Energy Information Administration
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Table 1, 2024 data, release date November 10, 2025. Utilities had 2,639 MW and IPP and CHP 215. The project's 1 to 3 GW (C06) is design nameplate, so the deck should not imply the plant is built.

claims.claim: Governor Dunleavy released a statement on Monday calling for data centers to be built in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: released a statement Monday calling for data centers to be built in the state.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
